answer:
English is almost impossible to avoid in everyday life nowadays. We hear it on television and in song lyrics, study it at school, and, for many of us, use it at work. This constant exposure gives us a fairly good sense of how the language works. I think most people understand at least some English, and quite a few probably have an excellent command of it. However, when I consider my own abilities, it is clear that some areas are more challenging than others. I feel more confident in the receptive skills—reading and listening—than in the productive skills of writing and speaking.

Throughout my years of studying English, first at primary school and then at secondary school, my teachers always emphasised writing. In upper secondary school especially, we wrote numerous essays and reviews. Yet despite all this practice, I still encounter difficulties. Spelling can be challenging, of course, but grammar is a greater concern for me. In my experience, grammatical problems are often complicated and harder to resolve than spelling difficulties, which can usually be settled by consulting a dictionary.

We did not get much reading practice at school. We had textbooks, of course, but the passages were often very short and covered unrelated topics, making them feel disconnected and out of context. In short, the textbooks were boring. In addition to these passages, we read several works of literature and wrote reviews of them. I think reading literature is a tremendously rewarding way to develop fluency in a language. This experience also proved valuable when I studied religious studies, as much of the required reading was in English.

My greatest difficulty with reading English arises when a text contains specialised terminology. Reading an English text that would be challenging even in Swedish is both demanding and time-consuming. This brings me to another problem: my patience, or rather, my lack of it. Naturally, reading in English takes longer than reading in Swedish, at least initially, but for some reason I find this hard to accept.

Speaking and listening are obviously closely related. Nevertheless, I find listening the easiest of the four skills and speaking the most difficult. This undoubtedly reflects the fact that I get far more practice listening, especially through television and music, than speaking. Although I do not understand every word, I can usually follow what is being said. However, specialised language presents difficulties in listening just as it does in reading.

As I mentioned earlier, speaking is my greatest challenge in English. I have had little practical experience because I have never spent an extended period abroad. At school, the teaching of English focused primarily, if not exclusively, on theory, so I had few opportunities to practise speaking there either. If anything, school can make students even more reluctant to speak: they become so concerned about getting the grammar right that they are afraid to open their mouths for fear of being laughed at. I know this sounds harsh, and it certainly does not apply to everyone. Nevertheless, I believe these fears would soon fade with regular speaking practice.

Having completed this assignment, I realise how difficult it is to assess my own abilities in the four language skills. I have never struggled to get good grades in English, but I firmly believe that grades rarely tell the whole story about what someone actually knows. What I do know is that learning a language involves many different skills, and I would like to improve in all of them.
